issue_context.title: Plannable Import: Support for_each
issue_context.body:
### Terraform Version

```shell
Terraform v1.5.4
on linux_amd64
```


### Use Cases

The ability to use `for_each` within an import block would greatly improve the use cases where the import block can be applied.

In complex scenarios, where you are importing resources in a variety of environments, to resources that use `for_each`, the current way that the import block can be used is very limited. You would basically need to define separate import blocks for every resource in every environment, which becomes so complex that it verges on being totally unusable.

In our use case in this scenario we use the traditional `terraform import` command and script the import outside of the Terraform plan. This works, but adds 'pre' steps that need to be done before a plan can be safely applied in migration scenarios, which adds complexity, as well as involving completely custom code that brings its own risks.

A logical extension of the functionality of the import block would be to add support for `for_each`. Then, in combination with the support for interpolation which was recently merged, this would potentially allow you to use the import block from the same 'source of truth' as you use to define the resources you are importing to.

This would greatly reduce the complexity of complex migration scenarios.

An example of this that I wrote on a [different issue](https://github.com/hashicorp/terraform/issues/33228) is:
Say you're managing 10 kubernetes clusters and are in the process of migrating to use Terraform to configure them.

Each cluster can have varying numbers of namespaces, with different names.

If you're planning to define the namespaces via a for_each based on some sort of logic (some values file, or variables or whatever), in this migration scenario it makes life so much easier if you can also define a for_each on the import block.

The alternative in the current scenario would be something like defining 10x import.tf files containing all the static import blocks for each cluster, and doing it that way, which is quite a painful process.

### Attempted Solutions

Something along these lines:

```
import {
  for_each = var.namespaces
  to = kubernetes_namespace.main[each.key]
  id = each.value.name
}

resource "kubernetes_namespace" "main" {
  for_each = var.namespaces
  metadata {
    annotations = {
      name = each.value.name
    }
    labels = each.value.labels
    name = each.value.name
  }
}
```

This does not work due to the lack of `for_each` support in the import block

### Proposal

Support the `for_each` argument in the import block to make something like the below possible:

```
import {
  for_each = var.namespaces
  to = kubernetes_namespace.main[each.key]
  id = each.value.name
}

resource "kubernetes_namespace" "main" {
  for_each = var.namespaces
  metadata {
    annotations = {
      name = each.value.name
    }
    labels = each.value.labels
    name = each.value.name
  }
}
```

### References

Requests for `for_each` support have been mentioned in (at least):
- #33228
- #33465
- #33389

review_comments:
I think an `import` block declared in a `.tf.json` file will end up in this case too, and `hcl.AbsTraversalForExpr` in that context has some interesting consequences.

In particular, `hcl.AbsTraversalForExpr` on a JSON `hcl.Expression` will expect a JSON string like `"aws_instance.foo"`, whereas normal expression evaluation would expect `"${aws_instance.foo}"`.

We can recognize whether a `hcl.Expression` originated in a JSON document by calling [`json.IsJSONExpression`](https://pkg.go.dev/github.com/hashicorp/hcl/v2/json#IsJSONExpression), which is really just a thin wrapper around a type assertion of the `json` package's unexported concrete expression type.

I think actually _handling_ a JSON expression once detected will probably require adding some new features to HCL's JSON package which we've considered a few times now but have so far always ended up finding an alternative:

The high-level idea is to expose a set of three methods in the package which take an expression for which `IsJSONExpression` would return `true` (panicking for any other expression, since that'd be a caller bug), and interprets the JSON expression in one of the following three ways:

1. As an evaluable expression, returning a `hclsyntax.Expression`:
    - a JSON object becomes a `hclsyntax.ObjectConsExpr` with the same function recursively applied to all of the nested values.
    - a JSON array becomes a `hclsyntax.TupleConsExpr` with the same function recursively applied to all of the nested values.
    - a JSON string gets parsed with `hclsyntax.ParseTemplate` and the result is returned. This should use equivalent logic to what the current `expr.Value` implementation does when given a non-nil EvalContext and evaluating a JSON string.
    - everything else (I think?) just gets trivially evaluated to a `cty.Value` and wrapped in a `hclsyntax.LiteralValueExpr`
2. As a static-analysis-friendly expression, also returning an `hclsyntax.Expression` but with one detail different than the previous item:
    - a JSON string gets parsed with `hclsyntax.ParseExpression` instead, and the result is returned.
3. As a literal, returning a `cty.Value` directly: we can technically already do this with` expr.Value(nil)`, but I'd propose adding a function specifically for it to complete this set and also make that possibility a little more evident in the package API. (Terraform uses this to ensure that `.tfvars.json` files are not subject to HCL template parsing/evaluation, for example.)

The three separate functions here reflect the three different ways a JSON value can be interpreted under the rules of the JSON variant of HCL. I think that would then allow some existing `json` package logic to be reimplemented in terms of the above three functions:
- `hcl.AbsTraversalForExpr`, `hcl.RelTraversalForExpr`, `hcl.ExprList`, `hcl.ExprMap`, and `hcl.ExprCall` with a JSON expression would interpret the given expression as case 2 above, and then call the same outer function again on the resulting `hclsyntax.Expression`.
- `expr.Value` for a JSON expression would interpret the given expression either as case 1 or case 3 depending on whether the given `EvalContext` is `nil`, and then call `Value` on the resulting `hclsyntax.Expression`.

But most importantly for what you were trying to do here, you'd also be able to directly call function 2 in this `exprToResourceTraversal` function if `json.IsJSONExpression` returns true, and then analyze the returned `hclsyntax.Expression` instead. This would, I think, effectively bridge the gap we've encountered many times now where the JSON syntax _is_ implemented in terms of `hclsyntax` but the translations it does are hidden in the unexported implementation. If we later also add functionality to `hclwrite` to take an `hclsyntax.Expression` and return an equivalent [`hclwrite.Expression`](https://pkg.go.dev/github.com/hashicorp/hcl/v2/hclwrite#Expression) then we'd have the building blocks required for a JSON-syntax-to-native-syntax translation tool, too.

If you come up with a more straightforward way to get there then of course it would be very reasonable not to take on a big reorganization of HCL's JSON syntax implementation as part of this project, but I offer the above in case it's useful since I expect the effort of implementing it will pay off in various other contexts too.

Thanks for jumping into this early @apparentlymart! I was about to start validating json input (which I unfortunately left til the end of course 🙄), and this gives me a good launching point when I find it doesn't work 😉

On further reflection I think I'd actually choose a different variation on function 3, for consistency with the others:

3. The same as cases 1 and 2 except that JSON strings get evaluated to their equivalent `cty.StringVal` and returned as `hclsyntax.LiteralValueExpr`.

This means that all three functions take a JSON expression and return a `hclsyntax.Expression`, and the only difference between them is what they do when encountering JSON strings. That string treatment is the essence of what makes string processing ambiguous in the JSON syntax and so I think it makes sense that it would be the only difference between these cases.

We could potentially still offer the variation that returns a `cty.Value` directly, since in that case it's guaranteed that the result will only include `cty.ObjectConsExpr`, `cty.TupleConsExpr`, or `cty.LiteralValueExpr` nodes in its entire subtree and so it's trivial to just call `Value(nil)` on the result to get that effect, but having three functions that all share an identical signature `func (hcl.Expression) hclsyntax.Expression` would make this more composable.

I ended up going with a proven method we've already used for now, so we don't need to invest in any updates to the hcl package yet. Since the `to` expression is always a single string in json, we can use the `expr.Value(nil)` trick to get the raw string and parse it again via hclsyntax.
I considered adding "legacy" fields to `ImportTarget` in https://github.com/hashicorp/terraform/pull/33618 but decided on the HCL synth kludge instead. Glad we are removing it.
